85f077699b.why: 'A model house' fixes the clarity note; nothing else changed. Worked out again: only all-parallel leaves two lit whichever bulb is removed. A series pair puts out its partner, a series third puts out all, and full series puts out all. Every arrangement lights all three at first. The T1 electric-circuits final asks no series or parallel question, so this is no re-ask.

91d63125a4.why: The dead lure (a fault cutting off all) is replaced by the series property students hand to parallel ('the same current'). That is false here: each branch draws its own. The key is re-keyed to the full voltage, so it no longer re-tests 85f077699b's independence. OpenStax: house and car devices are wired in parallel 'so that they utilize the full voltage of the source'. 'An equal share' is wrong because a share is a part; parallel branches each get the whole. 'Less current' is wrong: branches add current. One defensible answer.

85687baade.why: The stem's wording is fixed ('sit in two lamps plugged into sockets in the same house'). The card no longer calls a non-ohmic filament 'Ohm's law', and no longer teaches 91d63125a4's key; it says only that both get the same voltage. Key true, per OpenStax: on the same voltage the 60 W bulb draws more current, so its resistance is lower. The lures are truly wrong. 'More voltage' falls only with the unit's own parallel fact; the stem does not state it.

4acb975991.why: Quotation fixed. Popular Science Monthly (1913) gives Dove's account: 'in the Berlin Jahrbucher fur wissenschaftliche Kritik, Ohm's theory was named a web of naked fancies'. So 'a reviewer in a Berlin journal' is exact, and no one is named. Tell fixed: the key is no longer the plain negation of the stem. A longer wire with more current at the same push needs the fact that resistance grows with length; Ohm's own data had the current fall as the wire grew longer. The shorter, thicker and doubled-push results all fit. Each comparison reads naturally as the same metal with one thing changed. Ohm in Cologne, the 1827 book, Fechner in 1831 and the 1841 Copley Medal all confirmed.

54f93346d1.why: Fact-check fixed: 'the first electromagnetic motor, the first steady motion made from a current and a magnet' sits clear of the electrostatic motors of the 1740s. 'Most motors since' sits clear of reluctance and piezo motors. The RI notebook (4 September 1821) confirms the basin, the magnet and the wire circling the pole. The push is at right angles, so the wire circles rather than clinging or swinging away. This is the converse of T4's Oersted (current makes a field), not a re-ask.

af0a377cef.why: The two dead lures are replaced by live ones: 'never, since no wire joined the coils', and the half-truth 'connected, not disconnected'. 'When, if at all' keeps 'never' open, and 'connected or disconnected' is clearer than 'joined or broken'. Key true: transient deflections on making and breaking, opposite ways, none while the current is steady. 29 August 1831 and the iron ring confirmed. Henry published in 1832, with credit generally to Faraday. Not T4's electromagnet.

b080b04df5.why: Re-keyed off af0a377cef's fact onto the speed of change. OpenStax: 'The faster the motion, the greater the emf'. Demonstration guides report a bigger galvanometer deflection for a quicker push. A student repeats the test, so Faraday is not credited with a push he may not have made. The stem no longer teaches the ring question's key. The card's 'every generator' is narrowed to 'the generators in power stations', which is true: turbines spin the rotor inside the stator coils. Lures truly wrong. Caveat, not a fault: a strictly ballistic meter would throw the same; but the lure 'the same' gives the naive reason, not that one, and the grade-level fact is bigger.

f6ebfe36e7.why: The added question fills the scope's generator gap. The Faraday disc (diary, 28 October 1831) had a copper disc between the poles of a horseshoe magnet, contacts at the axle and the rim, and a galvanometer. It gave a continuous direct current while it turned: the first electromagnetic generator, of small voltage. The key is true. The lures are the over-reach of 'only a change makes a current' (one flick; only while speeding up) and 'the magnet must move', each wrong at a steady speed. It keys a mechanism beyond T1's 'a generator turns motion into electricity', and no other final asks it. The present tense for the machine fits the voice rule.

46b9eae5b9.why: 'Showed' replaces 'found', so Fontaine is not credited with the first discovery: Siemens (1867) and Pacinotti came first. Wikipedia: at Vienna in 1873 he 'carelessly connected the terminals of a Gramme machine to another dynamo' and 'its shaft began to spin'. 'Lifts her foot off the accelerator' fixes the pedal. Key true (regenerative braking), and friction brakes are still needed at low speed. Minor and left from before: 'working as a magnet, gripping the steel axle' is the weakest lure, but it was the judge's optional low note.
